questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Level of safety in country of destination and personal connection/interest in East Asia.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Chuo University provided a very clear timeline for deadlines and practical information before and upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Chuo University provided a great deal of assistance in answering any questions I had regarding arrival etc. I lived in the dorm at Tama Campus, and the Front Office was also very helpful. However, because I am a graduate student, I did not get all the orientation information that the undergrats got. I only received some of the information and not until a day prior to the particular events.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The application process going there is long (like any other study abroad). I think the fact that the university is located in Japan made it even more challenging because Japan has some pretty strict immigration rules. However, once all the practicalities were done, the process was fairly easy.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Dorm accommodation at Tama Campus. The accommodation is separated by gender and each gendered wing is separated into units of 6 people. Each unit has a shared shower room, two restrooms, and a small kitchenette and dining area. 

The residents of the dorm is a mix of Japanese students and international students which for me made the exchange experience way more authentic.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: No meal plans, but there was a big kitchen that all residents could use.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The university has three different campuses of which Tama Campus is the only one which is not located in the city centre. If you study something at the campuses in the city centre, the commute is quite long (compared to Denmark). I spent about 1 hour and 20 min. commuting each way on days when I had class. If you study something on Tama Campus, the housing is amazing. Other exchange students that took classes at Tama Campus loved it because they only had 5 min. walk to class.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I loved living in the dorms. The only inconvenience was that it is quite far from the city centre - especially when going to class. However, I do not regret living in the dorms. I made the most wonderful memories there and the best friends I could have imagined. It is also a game changer living with local students because they can teach you all about the culture and you get to cook a lot of Japanese food if you are interested in that. 

I was not in the city centre that much because of the distance, but campus is "only" an hour from Shinjuku Station (very central area), so it wasn't like I couldn't have gone there more often - I simply found that there were so many cool things to do in the outskirts and outside of Tokyo, so I didn't need it.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It is all online, so pretty easy. They also made a template so exchange students understand how to fill out the form.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The university was very helpful with most questions I had.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted. I found it a bit challenging understanding the course fact sheet because it is separated into graduate and undergraduate, but as an exchange student you can choose both. However, it seems to make a difference which one you choose in terms of credit transfer.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to have thoroughly looked at all the possible courses you can choose from and figure out how many credits the courses each represent at the University of Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I chose a mix of BA and MA courses because of a combination of my personal interest in the courses and for credit transfer reasons.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: More discussion-based classes at Chuo University with participation making up a big part of the final grade. They take attendance in class and expect you to participate actively during class, but there is less homework.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You have to pay health insurance in Japan too. No matter whether you have your own or not.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport and groceries were more expensive than I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There was a group of Japanese students in the dorm (Resident Assistants) whose job it was to make sure that the dorm was a nice place to live. They also arranged social activities, e.g. sports day, summer festival, cooking competition between countries, and curry dinner. 

The university also provided a space where students could exchange culture and language.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: EVERYTHING! Seriously, the more you socialise the better. You never know when or where you will make new friends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go outside of Tokyo. The city is great and should definitely also be experienced, but Japan is so much more than just Tokyo. There is a huge regional difference in Japan - from Okinawa all the way to Hokkaido.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Japan is very different from Denmark. I have travelled quite a lot in Asia before, so I was prepared for differences. However, there were still things I didn't expect. 

Some of the other exchange students from Europe found the adjustment very difficult.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Live in the dorms! Especially the one at Tama Campus is amazing.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They are (in my opinion) overly polite. They bow and say "thank you" all the time, and everything takes a long time because they double check everything. It seems very inefficient from a European perspective.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The orderliness. Everything is clean and organized. People are respectful and mindful if they bump into you on the train, and they keep quiet in public which was amazing to experience considering how massive Tokyo is and how many people live there.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. The application process is tough, so prepare yourself for that and be on top of deadlines - don't wait until last minute applying for official documents etc. I know that many people get stressed by this because they do it very close to the deadline. Being on top of deadlines gives you more room to relax during the application process. 

2. Consider housing thoroughly before you choose. There are pros and cons to living at Tama Campus vs. in the the city centre, so choose what is most appealing tom your needs. You have the change to be VERY social in the dorms, but if that is not for you, you might want to find some off campus housing in the city centre. 

3. Mentally prepare yourself for the exchange before going - what is it gonna be like living in another country? What style of teaching do the courses have? What do you want to get out of your exchange?

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is not a lot of courses in English, so check out the course catalogue before applying to make sure that you can obtain enough credits.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends that I made and the experiences and memories I got to share with them.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Keeping up with deadlines at my home university - course registration for the new semester etc. When you are on exchange, you don't think about courses back home, and since the semster is pushed a few months in Japan, it can be hard to keep up with deadlines at the end of the semester back home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
